Opening · Pistor 2013 (not assigned)

Law in the hierarchy of finance

“…the binding nature of legal and contractual commitments tends to be inversely related to the hierarchy of finance: Law tends to be binding on the periphery and relatively more elastic at the apex of the financial system.”p. 317
Apex
“This law-finance paradox tends to be resolved by suspending the full force of law where the survival of the system is at stake; that is, at its apex. It is here that power becomes salient.” (p. 315)
“major financial intermediaries received emergency liquidity support from the Fed or government bailouts” (p. 320)
Periphery
“It is thus at the periphery where default is most likely to result in involuntary exit.” (p. 320)
“homeowners faced personal bankruptcy and foreclosure in accordance with the law” (p. 320)
Pistor, “A Legal Theory of Finance,” Journal of Comparative Economics 41 (2), 2013: 315–330 · p. 315 is the abstract · p. 320 fragments are from one sentence on the United States after 2008

Part I · Hirschman 1970: 4

Two responses to decline

Albert O. Hirschman, 1945 · U.S. Army photograph (Sgt. Charles James), public domain
Exit
“(1) Some customers stop buying the firm’s products or some members leave the organization: this is the exit option. As a result, revenues drop, membership declines, and management is impelled to search for ways and means to correct whatever faults have led to exit.”
Voice
“(2) The firm’s customers or the organization’s members express their dissatisfaction directly to management or to some other authority to which management is subordinate or through general protest addressed to anyone who cares to listen: this is the voice option.”
Part I · Hirschman 1970

Economics and politics

  • “a more fundamental schism: that between economics and politics. Exit belongs to the former realm, voice to the latter.” (p. 15)
  • “Voice is political action par excellence.” (p. 16)
  • Exit in politics: “branded as criminal, for it has been labeled desertion, defection, and treason.” (p. 17)
  • Voice is used “whenever the exit option is unavailable” (p. 33, quoted in Sharafutdinova & Dawisha 2017: 363)
Monday demonstration, Leipzig, 23 October 1989 · Bundesarchiv, Bild 183-1989-1023-022 / Friedrich Gahlbeck, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE
The course PDF holds ch. 1 (pp. 1–20) only

Part II · Sharafutdinova & Dawisha 2017

Stationary bandits and Russia’s billionaires

“As Olson argued, stationary bandits have a stake in seeing their sovereign dominion grow and prosper and therefore they tax less, commit more credibly, and provide other public goods…”p. 362, citing Olson 2000
“Despite the growth in the number of billionaires in Russia, however, institutional quality only worsened and the cronyism within the executive branch increased.”p. 362
  • “35 percent of the country’s wealth is controlled by 100 or so oligarchs” (p. 365)
Moscow Exchange, main building, 2013 · Fitiss / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
Part II · Sharafutdinova & Dawisha 2017

Institutional arbitrage

“…business elites take advantage of weak institutions at home to make profits, while using strong institutions abroad to safeguard them. We call this phenomenon institutional arbitrage.”p. 363
  • “when exit is available at a relatively low cost, actors will choose it over voice” (pp. 363–64)
  • “The cost of voice in such countries—a defining characteristic of authoritarian regimes—far exceeds the cost of exit.” (p. 364)
Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland, Lausanne, 2008 · Archipat / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 (cropped)

Part II · Sharafutdinova & Dawisha 2017: 367–70

Round-tripping

  • “‘Round-tripping’ capital, i.e., when funds are transferred abroad first and then brought back into the country as foreign investment, is an important example of institutional arbitrage.” (p. 368)
Part II · Sharafutdinova & Dawisha 2017

London: courts, contracts, property

  • London Court of International Arbitration, London Commercial Court, Stockholm: “the most popular destinations” for dispute resolution (p. 369)
  • Berezovsky v. Abramovich, 2008–2012 · Cherney v. Deripaska, 2006–2012 (Table 3, p. 370)
  • “Most of the cases in the list are about the ownership of significant Russian domestic assets with no direct relationship to England.” (p. 370)
  • Commercial transactions “in contracts governed by English law” (p. 370)
  • London, 2006: “a fifth of all the prime real estate sold for above £8 million was bought by Russian buyers” (p. 367)
The Rolls Building, London: Royal Courts of Justice, Business and Property Courts, 2021 · Roger Green / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
Part II · Sharafutdinova & Dawisha 2017

“The best of both worlds”

“These business elites that take advantage of weak institutions at home for profit maximization rely on the best of both worlds—secure institutions in the West to protect profits over the long term and weak institutions in Russia to get super-profits in the short term.”p. 369
“‘A chicken can exercise ownership of eggs,’ he said, ‘and it can get fed while it’s sitting on the egg. But it’s not really their egg.’”Putin, as reported by Myers and Becker 2014, quoted on p. 371
Vladimir Putin at the congress of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, 17 December 2021 · kremlin.ru, CC BY 4.0

Part III · Applebaum 2024, Introduction and chs. 1–2

Kleptocracy

  • “Russia plays a special role in the autocratic network, both as the inventor of the modern marriage of kleptocracy and dictatorship and as the country most aggressively seeking to upend the status quo.”
  • “An influx of kleptocratic cash can also empower regimes to become more autocratic and repressive.”
  • Ch. 1: February 1970, West German and Soviet officials conclude the agreement for “the first gas pipelines from the U.S.S.R. to Western Europe”; Wandel durch Handel, “change through trade”
  • “Autocracy, Inc., offers its members not only money and security but also something less tangible: impunity.”

Midterm review · study guide, Part B

Four essay questions

  1. Explain the logic of a spin dictatorship. Why would a dictator give up mass violence, and under what conditions does spin work better than fear? Apply the model to one case it fits and one case it does not.terms 9, 10, 15–17
  2. What is the nature of economic growth under dictatorship?terms 10–15
  3. Has globalization made autocracy weaker or stronger?terms 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 15, 17, 19, 20
  4. Are Africa’s recent coups evidence that Africans are turning against democracy?terms 1, 4, 17, 18
  • Two of these four will be on the exam and you will answer both. Each answer: about 2–3 paragraphs.

Extra · Depth · Logvinenko 2021

Global Finance, Local Control

“…financial internationalization allowed local elites to raise capital from foreign investors while maintaining control over local assets. They legitimized their wealth using Western institutions, but they did so on their terms.”
“…without strong domestic rule-of-law protections, financial internationalization entrenches oligarchic capitalism and strengthens authoritarian regimes.”
  • Sharafutdinova & Dawisha 2017, n. 25: “For an extension of this argument linking capital mobility and authoritarianism, see Logvinenko 2013.”
